scenario: A company operates an e-commerce platform that must continue to accept orders even if one Availability Zone fails. Which characteristic of the AWS Cloud BEST enables this outcome?
wrong_answer_2: Trade capital expense for variable expense
correct_explanation: High availability — implemented by spreading workloads across multiple AZs — keeps the application accepting orders even when one data center fails. AWS Regions are designed with multiple AZs specifically to enable this resilience.
wrong_explanation_1: Pay-as-you-go pricing is a billing model; it does not by itself provide resilience to AZ failure.
wrong_explanation_2: CapEx-to-OpEx describes financial classification of spend, not technical resilience.
wrong_explanation_3: Economies of scale describe price reductions through scale, unrelated to surviving an AZ failure.

scenario: A workload's compliance and latency requirements are equally satisfied by two AWS Regions. Engineering wants to choose the Region with the lowest on-demand EC2 prices. Which factor are they evaluating?
wrong_answer_2: Number of edge locations in the Region
correct_explanation: EC2 and other AWS service prices vary by Region. When compliance and latency are equally met by multiple candidates, choosing the Region with the lower service price is a legitimate cost-optimization decision.
wrong_explanation_1: Service availability is a different factor — both candidate Regions presumably offer the required services in this scenario.
wrong_explanation_2: Edge locations are part of CloudFront's global network and are not a per-Region selection criterion.
wrong_explanation_3: IAM is global and available in every Region. It is not a differentiating selection factor.

scenario: Which statement BEST captures AWS's commitment to its customers' security under the AWS shared responsibility model?
correct_answer: AWS is responsible for the security OF the cloud (infrastructure, hardware, facilities), and the customer is responsible for security IN the cloud
wrong_answer_1: AWS owns all security responsibilities, leaving the customer with none
wrong_answer_2: Customers own all security responsibilities, including the physical hardware
wrong_answer_3: Security is fully outsourced to AWS Support when a Business Support plan is purchased
correct_explanation: The shared responsibility model divides security into AWS's responsibility for the cloud (physical infrastructure, facilities, hardware, hypervisor, managed services) and the customer's responsibility in the cloud (data, IAM, OS configurations, networking choices). Both parties have ongoing obligations.
wrong_explanation_1: Customers retain meaningful responsibilities — data protection, identity, and configuration — that AWS cannot perform on their behalf.
wrong_explanation_2: Customers do not own the physical hardware or facilities. AWS is responsible for those.
wrong_explanation_3: Support plans provide help with operational issues but do not transfer security responsibility from the customer to AWS.

scenario: A product team can now ship features in days rather than months by using AWS-managed services and on-demand provisioning. Which AWS Cloud value is this team realizing?
correct_explanation: Faster provisioning and managed services let teams experiment and ship more frequently — translating into faster innovation cycles. This is one of the core promises of cloud adoption.
wrong_explanation_1: Cloud adoption does not reduce data durability; AWS storage services offer industry-leading durability.
wrong_explanation_2: Cloud adoption does not weaken compliance posture; AWS supports many compliance programs.
wrong_explanation_3: Fixed quarterly planning is the legacy model the cloud's elasticity replaces.

scenario: Which AWS infrastructure component is responsible for serving cached content closer to viewers and is the foundation of Amazon CloudFront's worldwide delivery network?
correct_explanation: Edge locations form the CloudFront global network. There are hundreds of them worldwide — more than Regions — and they cache content close to end users to reduce latency for static and dynamic delivery.
wrong_explanation_1: Outposts racks are customer-located AWS hardware for hybrid workloads, unrelated to CloudFront edge caching.
wrong_explanation_2: AZs host customer compute and storage but are not CloudFront's edge-caching layer.
wrong_explanation_3: Regions are the geographic groupings of AZs. They host workloads but are not the CloudFront edge network.

scenario: Which of the following is NOT one of the six advantages of cloud computing typically cited by AWS?
correct_answer: Manual capacity planning at fixed annual intervals
wrong_answer_1: Trade capital expense for variable expense
wrong_answer_2: Benefit from massive economies of scale
correct_explanation: Manual fixed-interval capacity planning is the OLD on-premises model. The six AWS-cited advantages are: trade CapEx for variable expense; benefit from economies of scale; stop guessing capacity; increase speed and agility; stop spending money on data centers; and go global in minutes. Manual annual planning is the opposite of these benefits.
wrong_explanation_1: Trading CapEx for variable expense is one of the six benefits.
wrong_explanation_2: Benefiting from massive economies of scale is one of the six benefits.
wrong_explanation_3: Increasing speed and agility is one of the six benefits.

scenario: A CFO asks how the AWS pricing model differs from traditional on-premises infrastructure procurement. Which of the following statements is MOST accurate?
correct_answer: AWS bills based on actual consumption, while on-premises typically requires capital purchases of fixed capacity
wrong_answer_1: AWS bills are always fixed monthly amounts regardless of usage
wrong_answer_2: AWS requires customers to purchase three years of capacity up front
wrong_answer_3: On-premises infrastructure has no facilities cost, while AWS does
correct_explanation: AWS pay-as-you-go billing reflects actual consumption. Traditional on-premises infrastructure requires capital purchases of fixed capacity, often sized for peak demand and depreciated over years.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS bills vary with usage; they are not fixed by default.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS does not require multi-year prepayment to use the platform. Commitments are optional cost-saving mechanisms.
wrong_explanation_3: On-premises facilities (real estate, power, cooling) carry significant cost — they do not disappear in the on-premises model. AWS bundles those costs into service pricing rather than passing them as separate line items.

scenario: An EC2 instance is terminated after running for two hours. The customer is billed only for those two hours of usage and nothing else. Which AWS pricing fundamental does this illustrate?
correct_answer: Pay only for what you use
wrong_answer_1: Pay a fixed monthly fee regardless of usage
wrong_answer_2: Pay an annual subscription regardless of usage
wrong_answer_3: Pay an upfront fee plus hourly usage on top
correct_explanation: AWS pay-as-you-go pricing means customers pay only for the consumed resources during the time they were used. Two hours of EC2 use results in two hours of EC2 charges, with no minimums or termination fees for On-Demand instances.
wrong_explanation_1: Fixed monthly billing regardless of usage describes legacy hosting models, not AWS On-Demand.
wrong_explanation_2: An annual subscription regardless of usage is not the default AWS pricing model.
wrong_explanation_3: Upfront fees apply to optional commitment models like RIs and All Upfront Savings Plans, not to default On-Demand billing.

scenario: A finance officer notices that the per-GB cost of S3 storage decreases as the company's monthly storage volume grows past several tiers. Which AWS pricing fundamental does this illustrate?
correct_answer: Pay less when you use more (tiered pricing)
wrong_answer_1: Always pay the same per-unit price regardless of volume
wrong_answer_2: Pay only with annual upfront commitments
wrong_answer_3: Pay more as you use more (penalty pricing)
correct_explanation: AWS tiered (volume-based) pricing reduces the per-unit price at higher monthly usage tiers for many services, including S3 storage and data transfer. Customers "pay less when you use more".
wrong_explanation_1: AWS pricing is tiered, not flat per-unit, so per-unit cost can fall as volume grows.
wrong_explanation_2: Annual upfront commitments are optional Savings Plans, not the only way to get lower prices.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS pricing does not include penalty pricing for high usage; it provides volume discounts.

scenario: AWS has reduced its prices many times since launch. Which AWS Cloud benefit BEST explains why this is possible?
correct_answer: Massive economies of scale that lower AWS's per-unit cost over time
wrong_answer_2: Reduced focus on reliability and customer support
wrong_answer_3: Outsourcing of all infrastructure to third parties
correct_explanation: As AWS scale grows, per-unit infrastructure cost falls and AWS passes these savings to customers as price reductions on services. This is the direct expression of the "economies of scale" benefit.
wrong_explanation_1: There is no customer-mandated price ceiling. Prices reflect AWS's costs and competitive dynamics.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS has not reduced focus on reliability; investment in availability and support has increased over time.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS designs and operates its own infrastructure rather than outsourcing it.

scenario: A company expects to fully utilize AWS over the next three years and is willing to commit to a steady level of EC2 usage in exchange for a discount. Which approach BEST aligns with AWS Cloud economics?
correct_answer: Purchase a three-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan
wrong_answer_1: Run all EC2 workloads on Spot Instances
wrong_answer_2: Buy and depreciate physical EC2 hardware in a private data center
wrong_answer_3: Refuse to use any AWS service that requires a commitment
correct_explanation: Long-term, predictable EC2 usage maps neatly to a three-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan, which provides significant discounts (up to ~72%) in exchange for a usage commitment. It is the most economically aligned option for steady utilization.
wrong_explanation_1: Spot is suited to fault-tolerant workloads, not steady production usage that cannot be interrupted.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS does not sell physical EC2 hardware for customers to depreciate. Cloud economics replace this model.
wrong_explanation_3: Refusing commitment-based discounts forgoes the substantial savings the scenario could realize.

scenario: A team wants to assess how well their workload aligns with the six AWS Well-Architected pillars using a structured review. Which AWS service provides a free self-service workflow for this?
correct_explanation: The AWS Well-Architected Tool guides teams through a structured review of their workloads against the six pillars (operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, sustainability), producing a documented assessment and improvement plan at no charge.
wrong_explanation_1: Trusted Advisor offers best-practice checks but does not implement a full Well-Architected Framework review with documented pillars.
wrong_explanation_2: Compute Optimizer recommends resource right-sizing. It is not a Well-Architected workflow.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Config tracks resource configurations and rules, not Well-Architected pillar assessments.

scenario: A team places an Amazon SQS queue between a producer service and a consumer service so that the producer can keep submitting work even when the consumer is being deployed. Which Well-Architected design principle does this illustrate?
wrong_answer_2: Centralizing authorization at the API gateway
wrong_answer_3: Co-locating producer and consumer on the same EC2 host
correct_explanation: Inserting a queue between producer and consumer is a textbook loose-coupling pattern. Producers and consumers can be deployed, scaled, and operated independently because they communicate asynchronously through SQS rather than via direct synchronous calls.
wrong_explanation_1: Vertical scaling addresses sizing of a single resource, not coupling between services.
wrong_explanation_2: Centralizing authorization is a separate concern; it does not address coupling between producer and consumer at deploy time.
wrong_explanation_3: Co-locating producer and consumer increases coupling and shared blast radius — the opposite of the principle.

scenario: A team configures EC2 Auto Scaling, scheduled scaling for predictable peaks, and target-tracking scaling for variable load. Which Well-Architected design principle is the team applying?
wrong_answer_1: Implement a single static instance per workload
wrong_answer_3: Centralize all workloads on one EC2 instance
correct_explanation: Implementing elasticity — adding capacity when demand grows and removing it when demand falls — is core to the performance efficiency and reliability pillars. Auto Scaling with scheduled and target-tracking policies is a canonical implementation.
wrong_explanation_1: A single static instance is the opposite of elasticity.
wrong_explanation_2: Managed services are encouraged by Well-Architected, not avoided.
wrong_explanation_3: Concentrating all workloads on one EC2 instance creates a single point of failure and the opposite of elasticity.

scenario: A security team replaces ad-hoc local user accounts on EC2 instances with centralized identity, federated sign-in, and short-lived credentials issued by IAM roles. Which Well-Architected design principle does this implement?
correct_explanation: A strong identity foundation is a security pillar principle. It includes least privilege, centralized identity (federation), short-lived credentials, and avoiding long-term static credentials — exactly what the team has done.
wrong_explanation_1: Right-sizing is a cost-optimization principle, unrelated to identity strategy.
wrong_explanation_2: Testing recovery procedures is a reliability principle, not an identity-foundation principle.
wrong_explanation_3: Stop guessing capacity is about elastic scaling, not identity.

scenario: A platform team commits to managing every change to their AWS environment through a code-reviewed CloudFormation pipeline. Manual console changes are not permitted. Which Well-Architected design principle is BEST illustrated by this practice?
correct_explanation: Forbidding manual changes and codifying every change through code-reviewed templates is the canonical "perform operations as code" principle of operational excellence. Code is reviewable, repeatable, and auditable.
wrong_explanation_1: Consumption model is a cost-optimization principle about paying for what you use.
wrong_explanation_2: Small reversible changes is also operational excellence, but it focuses on deployment frequency and rollback ability, not on codification specifically.
wrong_explanation_3: Capacity planning is unrelated to manual-vs-code change management.

scenario: A team holds regular retrospectives, refines their runbooks based on past incidents, and revises CloudFormation templates over time. Which Well-Architected design principle do these practices illustrate?
correct_answer: Continuous improvement (evolve and improve over time)
correct_explanation: Continuous improvement across the Well-Architected pillars means learning from incidents, refining runbooks and templates, and evolving the workload over time. Retrospectives and runbook revisions are direct examples.
wrong_explanation_1: Failing forward without learning is the opposite of continuous improvement.
wrong_explanation_2: Freezing infrastructure prevents the very evolution Well-Architected encourages.
wrong_explanation_3: Skipping post-mortems eliminates a primary source of improvement.

scenario: Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for ensuring that a custom Amazon Machine Image (AMI) the customer builds is patched and free of vulnerabilities before it is launched?
wrong_answer_3: Shared between AWS and the customer
correct_explanation: Custom AMIs are customer artifacts. The customer is responsible for the OS image's patch level, embedded software, and configurations. AWS provides the EC2 service and base AMIs, but custom AMIs are entirely customer-managed.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS is not responsible for customer-built AMIs. AWS-managed AMIs (like Amazon Linux) are maintained by AWS, but customer images are not.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Marketplace publishes vendor AMIs; the vendor maintains those. Customer-built AMIs are the customer's responsibility.
wrong_explanation_3: Custom AMIs are entirely the customer's responsibility, not shared.

scenario: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which of the following is solely AWS's responsibility?
correct_answer: Ensuring the availability of AWS Regions and Availability Zones
wrong_answer_1: Choosing which AWS Region to deploy a workload in
wrong_answer_2: Configuring multi-AZ replication for a customer's RDS database
wrong_answer_3: Designing the customer's disaster recovery plan
correct_explanation: AWS owns and operates the physical infrastructure underlying every Region and AZ. Availability of those facilities is solely AWS's responsibility. Customers make architectural choices that benefit from that infrastructure.
wrong_explanation_1: Region selection is a customer decision based on compliance, latency, cost, and service availability.
wrong_explanation_2: Enabling Multi-AZ on RDS is a customer configuration choice, not AWS's responsibility.
wrong_explanation_3: DR design is a customer responsibility, even though AWS provides building blocks like Backup, cross-Region replication, and snapshots.

scenario: An application uses Amazon DynamoDB. Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for controlling which IAM principals can read or write to the DynamoDB tables?
correct_explanation: Although DynamoDB is fully managed, access control to customer data is the customer's responsibility. The customer configures IAM policies that grant or deny principals access to specific tables, items, and operations.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS operates the DynamoDB service but does not decide which principals may access customer data.
wrong_explanation_2: Support helps with operational issues but does not configure customer authorization policies.
wrong_explanation_3: Internal AWS service teams do not configure customer-side IAM policies.

scenario: A team enables encryption in transit for an Amazon EFS file system by configuring the NFS client to use TLS. Under the shared responsibility model, whose responsibility is it to configure the client side of in-transit encryption?
wrong_answer_2: Shared between AWS and the customer with AWS performing the bulk of the work
correct_explanation: AWS provides the encryption capability and the EFS mount helper that supports TLS, but the customer is responsible for configuring the client side — choosing to enable TLS in the mount, managing the client's CA trust, etc.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS does not configure the customer's NFS clients on their behalf.
wrong_explanation_2: Client-side configuration is solely the customer's responsibility, not split.
wrong_explanation_3: Upstream kernel maintainers are not part of the AWS shared responsibility model.

scenario: A security architect needs to centrally configure AWS WAF web ACLs, AWS Network Firewall rules, and Shield Advanced protections across many AWS accounts in an Organization. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this central security policy management?
correct_explanation: AWS Firewall Manager centrally configures and manages WAF, AWS Network Firewall, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall, and Shield Advanced protections across multiple accounts and resources in an AWS Organization. It is the dedicated cross-account security policy management service.
wrong_explanation_1: Security Hub aggregates security findings but does not centrally manage WAF or Network Firewall configurations.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS Config aggregators consolidate configuration data across accounts but do not push firewall rules.
wrong_explanation_3: Trusted Advisor offers recommendations; it does not centrally manage firewall configurations.

scenario: Which statement BEST describes "encryption in transit" as applied to AWS service usage?
correct_answer: Protecting data as it moves over the network — for example, using TLS between a client and an S3 endpoint
wrong_answer_1: Encrypting data only when it is written to storage volumes
wrong_answer_2: Encrypting only the database engine binaries on disk
wrong_answer_3: Encrypting CloudTrail event records archived to S3
correct_explanation: Encryption in transit protects data as it moves over the network — most commonly via TLS for HTTPS, NFS-over-TLS, or VPN tunnels. AWS endpoints support TLS, and many services have additional in-transit encryption features.
wrong_explanation_1: Encryption of data when written to storage is encryption AT REST, not in transit.
wrong_explanation_2: Encrypting binaries on disk is also encryption at rest at best, and unrelated to in-transit.
wrong_explanation_3: Encrypting archived CloudTrail records is also encryption at rest.

scenario: Which AWS service is the appropriate channel for an auditor to obtain AWS's current ISO 27001 certification?
correct_explanation: AWS Artifact is the on-demand portal for AWS's own third-party compliance reports and certifications, including ISO 27001, SOC 1/2/3, PCI-DSS reports, and more. Auditors download these reports directly from Artifact.
wrong_explanation_1: Audit Manager helps customers audit their own AWS usage. It does not provide AWS's external certifications.
wrong_explanation_2: Security Hub aggregates security findings within the customer's accounts. It does not provide AWS's external certifications.
wrong_explanation_3: re:Post is a community Q&A site; it does not host AWS certifications.

scenario: A company wants to centralize management of encryption keys used to protect Amazon EBS volumes, S3 objects, and RDS databases, with the ability to control who can use each key. Which AWS service is the appropriate choice?
correct_explanation: AWS KMS centrally creates and controls cryptographic keys used to encrypt EBS volumes, S3 objects, RDS data, and many other AWS resources. Key policies and IAM combine to control which principals can use a key.
wrong_explanation_1: Secrets Manager handles application secrets like passwords. It does not manage data-encryption keys used by AWS services.
wrong_explanation_2: Parameter Store stores configuration values; it is not the dedicated AWS encryption-key service.
wrong_explanation_3: ACM manages TLS certificates, not data-encryption keys.

scenario: A security administrator wants to enforce that all IAM user passwords are at least 14 characters long, must include a number and a symbol, and must expire after 90 days. Which IAM feature should the administrator configure?
correct_explanation: The IAM account password policy controls minimum length, character composition, expiration, and reuse prevention for IAM user passwords. It is the appropriate mechanism for these complexity and rotation requirements.
wrong_explanation_1: Permissions boundaries cap what permissions can be granted to an identity; they do not configure password rules.
wrong_explanation_2: SCPs restrict permissions across an Organization; they do not configure password complexity.
wrong_explanation_3: Role trust policies define who can assume a role. They do not configure passwords.

scenario: A platform team allows application developers to create their own IAM roles for Lambda functions but wants to ensure that the roles can never grant permissions outside an approved set (for example, no S3 wildcard access). Which IAM feature limits the maximum permissions that any role a developer creates can have?
wrong_answer_1: Resource-based policy on each S3 bucket
wrong_answer_3: Identity-based policy attached to the developer
correct_explanation: Permissions boundaries set the maximum permissions a principal can have, regardless of the identity-based policies attached. Requiring developers to attach a specific boundary to roles they create enforces an upper limit on those roles' capabilities.
wrong_explanation_1: Per-bucket resource policies control access to specific resources but do not cap what permissions a created role can be granted across the account.
wrong_explanation_2: Access-key rotation addresses credential hygiene; it does not bound permissions.
wrong_explanation_3: An identity-based policy on the developer grants their permissions but does not cap what roles they may create.

scenario: Account A wants to allow an IAM user in Account B to read objects in its S3 bucket. What is the recommended approach?
correct_answer: Create an IAM role in Account A that Account B can assume, with permission to read the bucket
wrong_answer_1: Share Account A's IAM user access keys with Account B
wrong_answer_2: Make the S3 bucket public so any AWS user can access it
wrong_answer_3: Disable IAM in Account A and rely on bucket ACLs
correct_explanation: Cross-account access is recommended via IAM role assumption. Account A defines a role that trusts Account B; users in Account B assume the role and receive short-lived credentials to access the bucket. This avoids shared keys and provides full audit logging.
wrong_explanation_1: Sharing long-term access keys is a security anti-pattern. Keys cannot easily be revoked per-person and are difficult to audit.
wrong_explanation_2: Making the bucket public exposes it to the entire internet, not just Account B. It violates least privilege.
wrong_explanation_3: Disabling IAM is impossible and would not solve the cross-account problem.

scenario: A company needs a managed Microsoft Active Directory in AWS to join Windows EC2 instances to a domain and authenticate users from an existing on-premises AD via trust. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_answer: AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory (AWS Managed Microsoft AD)
correct_explanation: AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a fully managed Microsoft Active Directory service. It supports domain-joining EC2 Windows instances, applying group policies, and creating trust relationships with on-premises AD — purpose-built for the scenario.
wrong_explanation_1: Cognito user pools authenticate end users of custom applications, not Windows domain machines.
wrong_explanation_2: IAM Identity Center provides SSO across AWS accounts but is not a managed Active Directory.
wrong_explanation_3: KMS manages encryption keys and is unrelated to Active Directory.

scenario: Which of the following correctly describes the difference between identity-based policies and resource-based policies?
correct_answer: Identity-based policies attach to IAM users, groups, or roles; resource-based policies attach directly to a resource such as an S3 bucket or KMS key
wrong_answer_1: Identity-based policies are always inline; resource-based policies are always managed
wrong_answer_2: Resource-based policies apply only to global services like IAM and Route 53
wrong_answer_3: Identity-based policies grant cross-account access automatically; resource-based policies cannot
correct_explanation: Identity-based policies attach to IAM principals (users, groups, roles) and define what those principals can do. Resource-based policies attach directly to a resource (e.g., S3 bucket policy, KMS key policy) and define who can do what to that specific resource — including principals from other AWS accounts.
wrong_explanation_1: Identity-based policies can be inline or managed; resource-based policies can also be considered standalone configurations on resources. The inline-vs-managed distinction is a separate concept.
wrong_explanation_2: Resource-based policies apply to many specific resources (S3 buckets, KMS keys, SQS queues, etc.), not only global services.
wrong_explanation_3: Cross-account access is most often achieved through resource-based policies combined with identity-based policies — not solely identity-based policies.

scenario: Which AWS service is INCLUDED FREE in every AWS account and provides baseline protection against common network and transport-layer DDoS attacks?
correct_explanation: AWS Shield Standard is automatically enabled for all AWS customers at no extra charge. It defends against common network- and transport-layer DDoS attacks such as SYN floods and reflection attacks.
wrong_explanation_1: Shield Advanced is a paid tier with more sophisticated mitigation and 24/7 access to the AWS Shield Response Team.
wrong_explanation_2: WAF is a paid application-layer firewall, not a free baseline DDoS protection.
wrong_explanation_3: GuardDuty is a paid threat detection service. It is not the free baseline DDoS mitigation product.

scenario: A team needs a managed network firewall service that filters traffic entering and leaving their VPCs at the perimeter, supporting stateful rules and integration with managed threat-intelligence rule groups. Which AWS service should they use?
correct_explanation: AWS Network Firewall is a managed VPC-perimeter firewall that supports stateful packet inspection, custom rules, and managed rule groups for threat intelligence. It sits in customer VPCs and filters east-west and north-south traffic at the network layer.
wrong_explanation_1: WAF protects HTTP applications at Layer 7. It is not a VPC-perimeter network firewall.
wrong_explanation_2: GuardDuty is a threat detection service, not an inline firewall that blocks traffic.
wrong_explanation_3: Security groups are per-instance virtual firewalls. They are useful but do not provide the centralized VPC-perimeter filtering with threat-intelligence rule groups that Network Firewall provides.

scenario: A team plans to run penetration tests against the company's own EC2 instances and Application Load Balancer. Which statement BEST reflects AWS's current customer support policy on penetration testing?
correct_answer: Customers may perform penetration testing on permitted AWS services against their own resources without prior approval, within the AWS penetration testing policy
wrong_answer_1: Penetration testing on AWS resources is never permitted
wrong_answer_2: Penetration testing requires submitting a request and receiving written approval each time
wrong_answer_3: Penetration testing is permitted only against other customers' resources
correct_explanation: AWS allows customers to perform security testing against a defined set of services on their own resources without prior approval, subject to the AWS Customer Support Policy for Penetration Testing. Out-of-policy activity (like simulated DDoS) still requires explicit authorization.
wrong_explanation_1: Penetration testing of one's own resources is explicitly permitted within policy.
wrong_explanation_2: Routine penetration testing within the policy does not require prior approval; only specific high-risk activities do.
wrong_explanation_3: Testing other customers' resources is prohibited; the scenario describes the company's own resources.

scenario: A developer wants a visual canvas to design a serverless application — composing Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB resources by dragging and connecting components — and have AWS generate the CloudFormation/SAM template automatically. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: AWS Application Composer is a visual builder for serverless applications. Developers drag and connect cards representing AWS services on a canvas, and Application Composer generates a CloudFormation/SAM template that can be deployed directly.
wrong_explanation_1: CodeStar is deprecated for new projects and offered project templates with a single dashboard, not a visual serverless designer.
wrong_explanation_2: CloudShell is a browser-based shell, not a visual application designer.
wrong_explanation_3: Cloud9 is a browser-based IDE for editing code, not a serverless drag-and-drop composition tool.

scenario: A new engineer wants to run AWS CLI commands without installing anything on her laptop. She wants a browser-based shell pre-authenticated with her AWS sign-in. Which AWS service should she use?
correct_explanation: AWS CloudShell is a browser-based shell pre-authenticated with the user's AWS Management Console identity. It comes with the AWS CLI and common scripting tools pre-installed. There is nothing to install on the laptop.
wrong_explanation_1: Cloud9 is a full browser-based IDE for code editing. While it also includes a terminal, the dedicated quick-CLI experience is CloudShell.
wrong_explanation_2: Session Manager opens a shell to an EC2 instance, not a general AWS CLI shell environment.
wrong_explanation_3: WorkSpaces provides full virtual desktops, much heavier than a browser-based CLI shell.

scenario: A team wants a fully featured browser-based IDE that supports editing source code, running terminal commands, and collaborating in real time with teammates. Which AWS service was historically purpose-built for this experience?
correct_explanation: AWS Cloud9 is a browser-based IDE with file editing, an integrated terminal, debugger support, and real-time pair-programming features. It is the AWS-native developer IDE-in-the-browser experience.
wrong_explanation_1: CodeBuild is a build service that compiles source code and runs tests. It is not an IDE.
wrong_explanation_2: CodeDeploy automates application deployments — it is not an IDE.
wrong_explanation_3: CodePipeline orchestrates CI/CD stages — it is not an IDE.

scenario: A team needs a private, managed Git repository service hosted within AWS so the source code never leaves AWS. Which AWS service was historically purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: AWS CodeCommit is a managed Git repository hosted in AWS. It supports standard Git workflows, IAM-based access control, and HTTPS/SSH access, keeping source code inside the AWS account.
wrong_explanation_1: CodeBuild compiles and tests source code. It is not a Git host.
wrong_explanation_2: S3 versioning provides object-level history but is not a Git server.
wrong_explanation_3: CodeArtifact is a package repository for build artifacts like npm, Maven, and PyPI packages — not a source-code Git host.

scenario: A platform team wants to publish a catalog of curated, parameterized application stacks (with vetted infrastructure templates) for application teams to self-service deploy in a standardized way. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this developer self-service platform?
correct_explanation: AWS Proton lets platform teams define and publish curated infrastructure and CI/CD templates that application developers can self-service. It is specifically designed for the platform-team / developer-self-service model.
wrong_explanation_1: Service Catalog publishes approved IT products but is broader and less tightly focused on developer self-service templates with infrastructure + pipelines compared to Proton.
wrong_explanation_2: CodePipeline orchestrates CI/CD stages but does not implement curated template self-service.
wrong_explanation_3: Systems Manager manages existing infrastructure operations; it is not a developer self-service catalog.

scenario: A multiplayer mobile game company in São Paulo needs single-digit-millisecond latency for game-server-to-player traffic. The nearest AWS Region is hundreds of kilometers away. Which AWS infrastructure offering should they consider FIRST?
correct_explanation: AWS Local Zones extend AWS infrastructure to specific metropolitan areas, providing compute and storage close to end users for single-digit-millisecond latency — the exact use case for latency-sensitive games in a city without a nearby Region.
wrong_explanation_1: Snowball Edge is a portable appliance for data transfer or constrained edge compute, not the right choice for hosting an always-on metro game server.
wrong_explanation_2: Direct Connect provides dedicated connectivity from on-premises to AWS; it does not place AWS compute closer to mobile end users.
wrong_explanation_3: Global Accelerator improves routing to AWS endpoints but does not place compute physically closer to a metro area.

scenario: A telecommunications partner deploys an AWS edge offering inside a 5G carrier network to enable ultra-low-latency applications for 5G subscribers. Which AWS offering does this describe?
correct_explanation: AWS Wavelength deploys AWS compute and storage at the edge of telecommunications carriers' 5G networks. This places workloads close to 5G subscribers without traffic leaving the carrier network, enabling ultra-low-latency applications.
wrong_explanation_1: Local Zones place AWS infrastructure in metro areas but are not embedded inside a carrier's 5G network.
wrong_explanation_2: Outposts deploys AWS infrastructure into a customer's data center, not a carrier 5G network.
wrong_explanation_3: CloudFront edge locations cache content; they are not deployed inside carrier 5G networks.

scenario: Which of the following lists the three core components of AWS global infrastructure correctly?
correct_answer: Regions, Availability Zones, and edge locations
wrong_answer_1: Subnets, security groups, and route tables
wrong_answer_2: VPCs, internet gateways, and NAT gateways
correct_explanation: AWS global infrastructure is described in terms of Regions (geographic areas), Availability Zones (isolated groups of data centers within a Region), and edge locations (the global content-delivery and DNS network).
wrong_explanation_1: Subnets, security groups, and route tables are VPC networking constructs within a Region — not the core global-infrastructure components.
wrong_explanation_2: VPCs, internet gateways, and NAT gateways are VPC components, not the global-infrastructure hierarchy.
wrong_explanation_3: IAM, KMS, and Route 53 are global services, but the question asks about infrastructure components — Regions/AZs/edge locations.

scenario: Which deployment design provides the HIGHEST fault tolerance within a single AWS Region?
correct_answer: Deploying redundant resources across multiple Availability Zones
wrong_answer_1: Deploying redundant resources across multiple subnets in a single AZ
wrong_answer_2: Deploying a single very large EC2 instance in a placement group
wrong_answer_3: Deploying resources only at edge locations
correct_explanation: Each AZ is an isolated set of data centers. Deploying redundantly across multiple AZs in the same Region provides the highest intra-Region fault tolerance — a single AZ failure cannot take down the workload.
wrong_explanation_1: Multiple subnets in the same AZ all share that AZ's fate. If the AZ fails, all those subnets go down.
wrong_explanation_2: A single large instance in a placement group is still a single instance; if it fails, the workload fails.
wrong_explanation_3: Edge locations are not deployment targets for customer applications.

scenario: A company needs a dedicated, private network connection from its on-premises data center to AWS — bypassing the public internet — to provide consistent network performance for large data transfers. Which AWS service should they use?
correct_explanation: AWS Direct Connect establishes a dedicated, private network link between an on-premises data center and AWS. It bypasses the public internet, offering consistent latency and throughput suitable for large or steady-state data flows.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Site-to-Site VPN traverses the public internet (encrypted). It does not provide a dedicated private link; performance varies with internet conditions.
wrong_explanation_2: Route 53 is a DNS service; it does not establish private network links.
wrong_explanation_3: Global Accelerator improves routing to AWS endpoints but does not provide a dedicated on-premises-to-AWS private circuit.

scenario: A company has years of on-premises backups stored on tape and wants to retain them in AWS for long-term archival, presented as a virtual tape library to the existing backup software. Which AWS service is the appropriate choice?
correct_explanation: AWS Storage Gateway's Tape Gateway presents AWS-backed storage as a virtual tape library (iSCSI VTL). On-premises backup software writes to virtual tapes that are stored in S3 and Glacier, replacing physical tape infrastructure.
wrong_explanation_1: Snowmobile is a now-rare exabyte-scale data transfer service in a tractor-trailer truck. It is not the right fit for ongoing virtual-tape-library replacement.
wrong_explanation_2: Direct Connect is a private network connection, not a tape library.
wrong_explanation_3: EBS is block storage attached to EC2 instances, not a virtual tape library presented to backup software.

scenario: A remote scientific field team needs to collect terabytes of data from sensors at a location with no reliable internet connection and later ship that data physically to AWS. Which Snow Family device is the BEST fit for this small-scale field collection?
correct_explanation: AWS Snowcone is the smallest Snow Family device — portable, rugged, and battery-powered — designed for small-scale data collection and edge compute in remote, often disconnected environments.
wrong_explanation_1: Snowmobile is an exabyte-scale truck-based transfer for massive datacenter-scale migrations, not portable field collection.
wrong_explanation_2: Snowball Edge Compute Optimized is larger and intended for heavier edge-compute workloads. Snowcone is the smaller field-portable choice.
wrong_explanation_3: Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads to S3 — it requires an internet connection, which the scenario explicitly lacks.

scenario: A team builds Docker images locally and needs a private, managed container image registry to push to and pull from at deploy time on Amazon ECS and EKS. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: Amazon ECR is a fully managed Docker / OCI container image registry. ECS and EKS integrate natively with ECR, and IAM controls access. It is the standard private container registry in AWS.
wrong_explanation_1: CodeArtifact stores package artifacts (npm, Maven, PyPI). It is not designed for OCI/Docker container images.
wrong_explanation_2: S3 versioning stores objects but is not designed as a container image registry with image manifest and authentication semantics.
wrong_explanation_3: CodeCommit is a Git source repository, not a container registry.

scenario: An application needs to convert text into natural-sounding speech in multiple languages, producing MP3 audio for an interactive voice response (IVR) system. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: Amazon Polly is the AWS text-to-speech service. It converts text to lifelike audio in many languages and voices, with output formats including MP3 — ideal for IVR and accessibility scenarios.
wrong_explanation_1: Transcribe is speech-to-text (the opposite direction).
wrong_explanation_2: Translate converts text between languages, not text to speech.
wrong_explanation_3: Lex is a conversational bot service that uses Polly for speech output, but the specific service that does TTS is Polly.

scenario: A photo-sharing application needs to automatically detect inappropriate content and recognize faces in user-uploaded images. Which AWS service is purpose-built for these image and video analysis tasks?
correct_explanation: Amazon Rekognition uses pre-trained machine learning to perform image and video analysis — object and scene detection, content moderation, face recognition, and more — without requiring ML expertise.
wrong_explanation_1: Comprehend is a natural language processing service for text, not images.
wrong_explanation_2: Textract extracts printed text and form data from documents. It is not a general-purpose image analysis service for moderation or face recognition.
wrong_explanation_3: SageMaker is for building, training, and deploying custom ML models. Using pre-trained Rekognition is the appropriate higher-level service for the stated tasks.

scenario: A data team needs a serverless ETL service to discover, catalog, clean, and transform data stored across S3, RDS, and Redshift, with managed crawlers populating a central data catalog. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: AWS Glue is a serverless ETL and data-catalog service. Crawlers populate the AWS Glue Data Catalog automatically, and jobs transform data using Apache Spark or Python shell — the canonical AWS service for batch ETL with cataloging.
wrong_explanation_1: Athena queries data in place using SQL but does not perform ETL pipelines or maintain crawlers (it consumes the Glue catalog).
wrong_explanation_2: Kinesis Data Firehose ingests streaming data to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, etc. It is not a batch ETL and cataloging service.
wrong_explanation_3: EMR runs managed Hadoop/Spark clusters that customers operate. Glue's serverless model and catalog focus distinguish it from EMR.

scenario: A business analyst wants to build interactive dashboards on top of data stored in S3, Redshift, and RDS, and share those dashboards with other internal users — without setting up servers. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this BI workload?
correct_explanation: Amazon QuickSight is the AWS managed BI service. It connects to many data sources (S3, Redshift, RDS, Athena, etc.), provides interactive dashboards, and supports sharing — without server management.
wrong_explanation_1: Athena is a query engine, not a dashboard product. QuickSight often sits on top of Athena.
wrong_explanation_2: EMR runs big-data clusters. It is not a BI dashboard service.
wrong_explanation_3: Glue is for ETL, not for dashboards.

scenario: A company needs an ENCRYPTED tunnel between an on-premises network and an AWS VPC over the public internet. The setup must be quick, with no dedicated circuit required. Which AWS service is the appropriate choice?
correct_explanation: AWS Site-to-Site VPN establishes an encrypted IPsec tunnel over the public internet between an on-premises VPN gateway and an AWS VPN gateway. Setup is fast and does not require ordering a dedicated circuit.
wrong_explanation_1: Direct Connect requires ordering a dedicated physical circuit through a partner, which is not quick. Direct Connect by itself is also not encrypted; encryption can be layered on top.
wrong_explanation_2: Route 53 is DNS; it does not provide encrypted on-premises connectivity.
wrong_explanation_3: PrivateLink provides private connectivity to specific AWS services and endpoints within AWS; it does not establish an on-premises VPN tunnel.

scenario: An IT governance team wants to publish a portfolio of approved CloudFormation-based products (e.g., a standard hardened Windows server, a vetted analytics stack) for internal developers to launch in a controlled, repeatable way. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: AWS Service Catalog lets administrators publish a portfolio of approved CloudFormation-based products. End users in the organization can launch those products in a controlled, repeatable way, while administrators retain governance over what is offered.
wrong_explanation_1: Marketplace catalogs third-party software for general AWS customers. It is not the internal-approved-portfolio service.
wrong_explanation_2: re:Post is a community Q&A site, not a launchable product catalog.
wrong_explanation_3: CodeArtifact stores build artifacts (npm, Maven, PyPI). It is not a CloudFormation portfolio service.

scenario: A small business wants on-demand access to vetted AWS-certified experts for one-off projects, paying via their AWS bill. Which AWS resource matches this gig-style engagement model?
correct_explanation: AWS IQ connects customers with AWS-certified third-party experts for short-term, scoped projects. Payments are processed through the customer's AWS bill, and the marketplace model fits gig-style engagements.
wrong_explanation_1: Professional Services is a paid AWS-employed consulting team. It is not the gig marketplace AWS IQ is.
wrong_explanation_2: AMS provides ongoing operations management for production workloads — much larger in scope than a gig project.
wrong_explanation_3: re:Post is free community Q&A, not a hire-an-expert marketplace.

scenario: A large enterprise wants AWS to take over day-to-day operations of its AWS production environment — patching, change management, incident response — under a contract. Which AWS offering provides this fully managed operations service?
correct_explanation: AWS Managed Services (AMS) takes over day-to-day operations of a customer's AWS environment under a contract. AMS handles patching, monitoring, change management, incident response, and other operations tasks following ITIL-aligned processes.
wrong_explanation_1: Professional Services delivers project-based consulting, not ongoing operations.
wrong_explanation_2: AWS IQ is a gig marketplace for short-term work, not full ops takeover.
wrong_explanation_3: Trusted Advisor produces recommendations; it does not operate the environment on the customer's behalf.

scenario: Which AWS pricing fundamental BEST describes the behavior in which the per-GB price of S3 storage decreases as a customer crosses higher usage tiers in a month?
correct_answer: Pay less when you use more
wrong_answer_1: Pay only for what you use
wrong_answer_3: Pay more as you scale (penalty pricing)
correct_explanation: "Pay less when you use more" is one of AWS's three pricing fundamentals (alongside pay-as-you-go and save when you reserve). It refers to tiered, volume-based discounts that reduce per-unit prices as monthly usage grows.
wrong_explanation_1: "Pay only for what you use" describes pay-as-you-go billing in general — not specifically the volume discount tier behavior.
wrong_explanation_2: "Save when you reserve" describes Reserved Instances and Savings Plans, which require a commitment. Tiered pricing applies automatically without commitment.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS pricing rewards higher usage with discounts, not penalties.

scenario: A company is calculating its data transfer costs for AWS workloads. Which of the following is generally FREE?
correct_answer: Inbound data transfer from the internet to AWS
wrong_answer_1: Outbound data transfer from AWS to the internet at high volumes
wrong_answer_2: Data transfer between AZs within the same Region
wrong_answer_3: Data transfer between two AWS Regions
correct_explanation: Inbound data transfer from the internet into AWS services is generally free. AWS charges instead for outbound data transfer, inter-AZ data transfer (for some services), and inter-Region transfer.
wrong_explanation_1: Outbound transfer is metered per-GB and is one of the larger cost components for many workloads.
wrong_explanation_2: Cross-AZ data transfer is charged for most services (for example, EC2 cross-AZ traffic).
wrong_explanation_3: Cross-Region transfer is charged. Free transfer is mostly limited to inbound from the internet.

scenario: A team is choosing between Standard and Convertible Reserved Instances for a one-year commitment. Which trade-off correctly describes the difference?
correct_answer: Standard RIs offer a larger discount but less flexibility; Convertible RIs offer a smaller discount but allow changing instance attributes
wrong_answer_1: Standard RIs are cheaper AND more flexible than Convertible RIs
wrong_answer_2: Convertible RIs require no commitment and provide the largest discount
wrong_answer_3: Standard RIs are billed hourly and Convertible RIs are billed monthly
correct_explanation: Standard RIs provide the highest RI discount but cannot be exchanged for a different instance family. Convertible RIs allow exchanging for RIs of equal or greater value but at a smaller discount. The trade-off is depth of discount versus flexibility.
wrong_explanation_1: There is no scenario where Standard RIs are simultaneously cheaper AND more flexible. The two attributes trade off.
wrong_explanation_2: All RIs require a 1- or 3-year commitment. Convertible RIs do not offer the largest discount; Standard RIs do.
wrong_explanation_3: Both RI types are billed similarly in terms of how the commitment is consumed. The hourly-vs-monthly framing is incorrect.

scenario: A customer's workload is consistently on EC2 instances within a single family (m5) and a single Region. Which pricing model offers the LARGEST discount while still matching this specific commitment?
correct_answer: EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the m5 family in that Region
wrong_answer_1: Compute Savings Plan for any compute service
correct_explanation: EC2 Instance Savings Plans commit to a specific instance family in a specific Region and offer the largest Savings Plan discount (up to ~72%) — larger than Compute Savings Plans, which are broader in flexibility.
wrong_explanation_1: Compute Savings Plans cover all of EC2, Lambda, and Fargate. The broader flexibility comes at a smaller maximum discount than EC2 Instance Savings Plans.
wrong_explanation_2: On-Demand has no commitment and no discount.
wrong_explanation_3: Spot offers the largest possible EC2 discount but instances can be reclaimed with two minutes' notice — unsuitable for a consistently-on workload.

scenario: A company has an AWS Organization with a management account and 25 member accounts. Reserved Instances purchased in one member account go unused. Which feature can help OTHER member accounts benefit from those Reserved Instances?
correct_answer: RI and Savings Plan sharing within the Organization (enabled by the management account)
wrong_answer_1: AWS Trusted Advisor automatically transfers the RIs
wrong_answer_2: AWS Service Catalog reassigns the RIs
wrong_answer_3: AWS Marketplace sells unused RIs back to AWS at full price
correct_explanation: AWS Organizations supports sharing of Reserved Instance and Savings Plan discount benefits across linked accounts. When sharing is enabled, unused RI capacity in one account can apply to matching usage in another account in the family.
wrong_explanation_1: Trusted Advisor flags underutilized RIs but does not redistribute them automatically.
wrong_explanation_2: Service Catalog publishes approved IT products; it does not redistribute RIs.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS does not buy back RIs at full price; customers can sell Standard RIs in the Reserved Instance Marketplace, but sharing across the Organization is the simpler answer.

scenario: In an AWS Organization, which statement BEST describes the relationship between the management account and member accounts?
correct_answer: The management account pays the consolidated bill and can apply SCPs to member accounts; member accounts are individual AWS accounts joined to the Organization
wrong_answer_1: The management account is a member account elected by AWS Support each year
wrong_answer_2: Member accounts can act as the billing payer for the management account
wrong_answer_3: Management and member accounts share a single IAM identity store automatically
correct_explanation: The management account (formerly "master account") creates the Organization, receives the consolidated bill, and can attach service control policies. Member accounts are otherwise independent AWS accounts that have joined the Organization.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Support does not elect a new management account annually. The management account is set when the Organization is created.
wrong_explanation_2: Member accounts cannot bill on behalf of the management account; billing flows from members to the management account.
wrong_explanation_3: Each AWS account has its own IAM identity store by default. IAM Identity Center can provide cross-account SSO, but this is configured, not automatic.

scenario: A company brings several proprietary software licenses (Oracle, SQL Server, etc.) to AWS and wants centralized tracking and enforcement of license usage to avoid out-of-compliance situations. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: AWS License Manager centralizes tracking and enforcement of software licenses (BYOL) across AWS and on-premises usage. Administrators define rules and limits, and License Manager prevents licensed deployments from exceeding the entitlement.
wrong_explanation_1: Cost Explorer analyzes spend, not license usage.
wrong_explanation_2: Marketplace sells third-party software but is not a license-tracking enforcement tool for BYOL.
wrong_explanation_3: Service Catalog publishes approved products; it is not a license-tracking service.

scenario: An administrator wants to view and request increases to AWS service quotas (formerly "service limits") across many accounts and Regions from a single console. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
wrong_answer_1: AWS Trusted Advisor service-limit checks only
correct_explanation: AWS Service Quotas is the central console for viewing and requesting quota changes for AWS services. It supports per-service and per-Region views and can integrate with CloudWatch for proactive quota monitoring.
wrong_explanation_1: Trusted Advisor has a service-limits check but is not the centralized management and adjustment tool that Service Quotas is.
wrong_explanation_2: Support is the historical path for limit increases but is not the dedicated service for browsing and requesting them — Service Quotas is.
wrong_explanation_3: Health Dashboard reports service events; it does not manage quotas.

scenario: Which of the following is INCLUDED in the AWS Basic Support plan available to all AWS customers at no additional cost?
correct_answer: Customer service, documentation, whitepapers, AWS re:Post, and a limited set of Trusted Advisor checks
wrong_answer_1: 24/7 access to Cloud Support Engineers via phone and chat
wrong_answer_3: Concierge Support for billing and account questions
correct_explanation: Basic Support is free and includes 24/7 access to customer service for account/billing questions, documentation, whitepapers, AWS re:Post, and a limited set of core Trusted Advisor checks. Technical support from Cloud Support Engineers requires a paid plan.
wrong_explanation_1: 24/7 access to Cloud Support Engineers begins with Business Support, not Basic.
wrong_explanation_2: Dedicated TAMs are exclusive to Enterprise On-Ramp and Enterprise Support plans.
wrong_explanation_3: Concierge Support is exclusive to Enterprise Support, not Basic.

scenario: An enterprise wants billing experts who help with account-level billing investigation, payment methods, and consolidated billing complications, included as part of their AWS Support plan. Which AWS Support tier includes this Concierge billing support?
correct_explanation: The Concierge Support team — a billing and account specialist team — is exclusive to AWS Enterprise Support. They assist with billing analysis, payment, and account-management questions for enterprise customers.
wrong_explanation_1: Basic Support does not include Concierge billing support.
wrong_explanation_2: Developer Support is a lower paid tier and does not include Concierge.
wrong_explanation_3: Business Support adds 24/7 Cloud Support Engineer access but does not include the Concierge team.

scenario: A company needs both procurement of third-party software via AWS billing AND access to short-term certified expert help. Which two AWS resources, respectively, BEST match these needs?
correct_answer: AWS Marketplace for software procurement; AWS IQ for short-term expert help
wrong_answer_1: AWS IQ for software procurement; AWS Marketplace for short-term expert help
correct_explanation: AWS Marketplace catalogs third-party software with consolidated AWS billing. AWS IQ connects customers with AWS-certified third-party experts for short-term scoped projects, also billed through AWS. The two together cover both needs.
wrong_explanation_1: The mapping is reversed: Marketplace is for software, IQ is for experts.
wrong_explanation_2: Service Catalog publishes approved products internally for an organization's own developers — it does not procure third-party software or expert engagements.
wrong_explanation_3: re:Post is free community Q&A, not a software or expert procurement channel.
